sysd-reliab-202.title: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation
sysd-reliab-202.text: If you can measure only four metrics of a user-facing system, measure these: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Latency is the time to service a request. Track successful and failed requests separately, since a fast HTTP 500 skews the figures and a slow error is worse than a fast one. Traffic measures demand, such as HTTP requests per second for a web service. Errors are requests that fail explicitly (HTTP 500s), implicitly (an HTTP 200 with wrong content) or by policy (slower than a committed one-second response). Saturation is how full the service is, emphasizing the most constrained resource. Many systems degrade before reaching 100% utilization, so a utilization target is essential. Rising latency is often a leading indicator of saturation, and the 99th percentile over a one-minute window can give a very early signal. Saturation also covers prediction, such as a database that will fill its hard drive in 4 hours. If you measure all four and page a human when one is problematic, the service is at least decently covered.

sysd-reliab-193.title: Choosing service level indicators: a handful, not everything
sysd-reliab-193.text: Pick too many indicators and nobody can tell which ones matter. Pick too few and significant behaviors go unexamined. Choosing indicators means selecting a handful of metrics that reflect what users want from the system, rather than every metric a monitoring system can track. Serving systems usually care about availability, latency and throughput. Storage systems care about latency, availability and durability, and big data pipelines about throughput and end-to-end latency. All systems should track correctness as an indicator of health. It is often a property of the data rather than the infrastructure, so it is usually not an SRE responsibility. Aggregation needs care: averaging requests over a minute may hide much higher instantaneous request rates in bursts that last only a few seconds. Standardizing SLI definitions avoids reasoning from first principles each time. That means fixing the aggregation interval, the aggregation region, the measurement frequency and which requests count.

sysd-reliab-194.title: Choosing SLO targets: start from users, not from today's numbers
sysd-reliab-194.text: Choosing targets is not a purely technical activity. Product and business implications shape the SLIs and SLOs, and SRE advises on the risks and viability of the options. Start from what users care about, not what is easy to measure, approximating their needs if necessary. Working backward from desired objectives to indicators often works better than the reverse. Do not pick a target from current performance. Adopting values without reflection can lock you into a system that needs heroic efforts to meet its targets and cannot improve without redesign. Keep as few SLOs as possible, just enough to cover the system's attributes, and defend each one. An SLO that never wins a conversation about priorities is probably not worth having. Avoid absolutes: a system that is always available and scales without added latency is unrealistic and costly to operate. Perfection can wait. Start with a loose target and tighten it, rather than set a strict one that must be relaxed once found unattainable.

sysd-reliab-188.title: Chaos engineering: breaking things on purpose
sysd-reliab-188.text: Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly picks a server and disables it during normal working hours. This is chaos engineering, the discipline of experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production. Engineers must build redundancy and automation that survive such failures without affecting users. The intent is to move from assuming no breakdowns to treating breakdowns as inevitable, making built-in resilience an obligation rather than an option. Resilience is the ability to tolerate failures while keeping quality of service. Teams often miss it for lack of time or domain knowledge. The Simian Army extends the idea. Chaos Gorilla drops a whole availability zone, and Chaos Kong drops an entire region. Game days purposely create major failures on a regular basis, inspired by firefighter training. Google's DiRT does the same for disaster recovery testing. One experiment on {{ref:sysd-reliab-050}} terminated random pods and used the pods' recovery time as the resiliency metric.

sysd-reliab-184.title: Business continuity planning: keeping the whole business running
sysd-reliab-184.text: Any event that could hurt operations belongs in a business continuity plan, from a supply chain interruption to the loss of critical computing and network resources. Business continuity planning is the process of creating systems of prevention and recovery to deal with potential threats. Its aim is that an organization can keep delivering products or services at acceptable levels after a disruptive incident. It is a subset of risk management. The plan outlines a range of disaster scenarios and the steps the business takes in each to return to regular trade. It is written ahead of time and can include precautions. Business continuity is the outcome of executing both the planning and {{ref:sysd-reliab-091}} properly. Continuity need not cover every activity. ISO 22301 requires organizations to define continuity objectives, meaning the minimum acceptable service levels and the maximum tolerable period of disruption. Plans are tested at three scales. Tabletop exercises involve a few people on one aspect. Medium exercises involve several teams, with pre-scripted surprises. Complex exercises add no-notice activation, actual evacuation and use of a recovery site.

sysd-reliab-097.title: High availability architectures: three ways to pair nodes
sysd-reliab-097.text:
High availability architectures pair a node with a standby, secondary or second primary so the service keeps answering when one node fails. In the CAP theorem, availability means every non-failing node can be queried. It returns a reasonable response within a reasonable time, with no error or timeout. That only guarantees a response, not that the data is the most up-to-date. A design target of 4-9's means the service is up 99.99% of the time and down at most 52.5 minutes per year.

In primary-backup, the backup is a stand-by that receives replicated data. On failure the switch to it is manual, and the idle backup may waste hardware. In primary-secondary, the secondary can serve reads to balance load. But replication latency means reads from it may be inconsistent with the primary. In primary-primary, both nodes handle reads and writes and replicate to each other, raising throughput. But if both update the same product, the final state can be unpredictable, so use it with caution. Pairing also helps the arithmetic: on Amazon EC2, which has 90% availability, a double-node architecture raises availability from 90% to 99%.

sysd-reliab-098.title: Observability: asking questions you did not plan for
sysd-reliab-098.text: Observability is the ability to ask arbitrary questions about a system without knowing ahead of time what to ask. Its three pillars are logging, tracing and metrics. Logging records discrete events, such as an incoming request or a visit to a database, and has the highest volume of the three. Teams define a standardized logging format so keywords can be searched across massive logs. Tracing is request-scoped. It follows one user request through the API gateway, load balancer, services and database, which helps identify bottlenecks. Metrics are aggregatable measurements such as service QPS, API responsiveness and latency, with raw data recorded in time-series databases like InfluxDB. Prometheus pulls the metrics, Grafana displays them, and the alert manager sends email, SMS or Slack notifications. OpenTelemetry unifies the three pillars in a single framework. Monitoring watches predefined sets of telemetry, whereas observability explores properties and patterns that were not defined in advance. Metrics and logs must be instrumented up front, so an unforeseen issue can require shipping new code.

sysd-reliab-104.title: Site reliability engineering: software engineering applied to operations
sysd-reliab-104.text: Site reliability engineering, or SRE, is a discipline that applies software engineering to IT infrastructure and operations. It aims to monitor and improve the availability and performance of deployed software systems. SREs are responsible for a combination of availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response and capacity planning. The discipline focuses on automation, system design and improved resilience, typically with an {{ref:sysd-reliab-147}} methodology. It is considered a specific implementation of DevOps that concentrates on building reliable systems, while DevOps covers a broader scope of operations. Common practices include automating repetitive tasks and defining reliability goals to prevent endless effort. Toil management is a principle: toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work. Reliability goals are defined and measured with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets. Other principles are defining, testing and running a process for managing incidents, and change and release management including CI/CD.

sysd-reliab-191.title: The 3-2-1 backup rule
sysd-reliab-191.text: Keep at least 3 copies of the data, on 2 different types of storage media, with one copy offsite in a remote location. That is the 3-2-1 rule. Different media avoid losses with similar causes: optical discs may survive being underwater while LTO tapes may not, and SSDs cannot suffer head crashes. An offsite copy, which can be cloud storage, protects against fire and natural disasters. No storage is perfect, so many experts also keep a second local physical copy. Ransomware can overwrite a backup drive that stays plugged in, so at least one backup medium should be disconnected when not in use.

sysd-reliab-209.title: Tiered backups: fast restores nearby, long memory far away
sysd-reliab-209.text: Backups do not matter, recovery does. The scenarios you must recover from should dictate the backup method, how often you take restore points, where you store backups and how long you keep them. The less recent data you can lose, the more serious an incremental strategy should be. The faster users must be rescued, the more local backups should be. A tiered strategy follows from both: frequent, quickly restored backups near the live datastores, and fewer, longer-retained backups on more remote, more independent storage. The first tier holds many frequent backups, retained hours to single-digit days and restored in minutes. It protects against most software bugs and developer error. The second tier holds fewer backups for single-digit or low double-digit days on local distributed filesystems, restoring in hours. Later tiers use nearline tape libraries and offsite media against site-level issues, and they are taken less often but retained longer. Reaching back further helps with low-grade corruption bugs found months later, but old backups may be unusable after code and schema changes. Google drew the line between 30 and 90 days.

sysd-reliab-192.title: Backing up live data: freeze it, then copy
sysd-reliab-192.text: Files being actively updated are hard to back up consistently. One way is to quiesce them, take a snapshot, resume live operations and back up the snapshot. A snapshot is an instantaneous filesystem function that presents a copy as if frozen at one point in time, often through a copy-on-write mechanism. Snapshotting a file while it changes yields a corrupted file, as does doing so across interrelated files such as a database. A database hot backup combines a snapshot of the data files with a snapshotted log of changes made during the backup. A restore applies the log to bring the copy up to when the backup ended.

sysd-reliab-094.title: Disaster recovery strategies: choosing the measures
sysd-reliab-094.text: The right recovery measure depends on the cost of downtime compared with the cost of implementing it. A disaster recovery strategy is the set of measures chosen to restore systems and data after a disaster. It derives from the business continuity plan, and a cost-benefit analysis picks the measures. Common strategies are backups to tape sent off-site, backups to disk on-site and copied off-site, and replication off-site. Cloud options include replicating metadata to a private cloud, hybrid cloud replication for instant fail-over, and disaster recovery as a service from a third-party vendor. Precautions include local mirrors, surge protectors, backup generators and fire prevention systems.

sysd-reliab-096.title: Disaster recovery practices: controls, tests and permissions
sysd-reliab-096.text: Every $1 spent on hazard mitigation, such as a disaster recovery plan, saves society $4 in response and recovery costs. Disaster recovery practices are the controls, tests and procedures that keep a plan working when a disaster happens. Controls are preventive, detective or corrective, and the plan records them. DR tests exercise them regularly, verify the plan and expose weaknesses or gaps. A cloud recovery strategy should be flexible enough for partial failures, such as recovering specific files, as well as full environment failures. Define who may execute the plan, and separate those permissions from access to backup data to limit unauthorized actions.

sysd-reliab-214.title: Testing data recovery before you need it
sysd-reliab-214.text: Components that are not continually exercised fail when you need them most. Recovery dependencies, mostly backups, can be latently broken without anyone knowing until recovery is attempted. So recovery must be tested continuously. Finding a broken restore process before you need it lets you take another backup, provision more resources or change the SLO. You only know you can recover your recent state if you actually do so. Manual staged tests become drudgery, so automate them and run them as part of normal operations. Alert when a recovery process stops sending a heartbeat of success. Only a full end-to-end test is proof enough. Check that backups are valid and not empty, and that resources suffice for setup, restore and post-processing. Check that recovery finishes in reasonable time and that progress is observable. Make sure no critical dependency lies outside your control.

sysd-reliab-208.title: Backups versus archives: built to be restored
sysd-reliab-208.text: People do not want backups, they want restores. The most important difference between backups and archives is that backups can be loaded back into an application while archives cannot. A backup effort should therefore focus on data recovery. Archives safekeep data for long periods to meet auditing, discovery and compliance needs. They need not recover within service uptime limits, and a week to retrieve logs for a month-long audit may be acceptable. Real backups must be recovered quickly, or users lose useful access from the onset of the problem until recovery completes. Teams define SLOs for data availability across failure modes and practice demonstrating they can meet them.

sysd-reliab-212.title: Data loss failure modes: 24 types to plan for
sysd-reliab-212.text: Data loss comes in 24 distinct types, and a restore plan must handle them in any combination. Losses may come from user action, operator error, application bugs, infrastructure defects, faulty hardware or site catastrophes. A loss may be big bang, such as 1 million rows replaced by 10 in a minute. It may be creeping, such as 10 rows deleted every minute for weeks. A study of 19 Google recovery efforts found that software bugs causing deletion or lost referential integrity were the most common user-visible loss. The hardest were low-grade corruption found weeks or months later.

sysd-reliab-213.title: Out-of-band validation: trust storage, but verify
sysd-reliab-213.text: Trust storage systems, but verify. Even consensus-based storage is not infallible in practice, so applications cannot know all their data is good until they check. Out-of-band data validation is a system of checks and balances within and between an application's datastores. It detects low-grade corruption or loss before it becomes unrecoverable. Speed matters because bad data propagates, with references to missing or corrupt data copied and links fanning out. The sooner a loss is known, the easier and more complete recovery is. Validation pipelines are often map-reduce or Hadoop jobs. They slow engineering in the short term but give developers courage to move faster later, much as unit tests do. Validators must be balanced: too strict and engineers abandon them, too lax and corruption slips through. Validate only invariants whose failure devastates users, such as file contents matching folder listings. At scale validators cost compute and lower cache hit rates, so tier them. Daily validators catch the most disastrous scenarios within 24 hours, and more rigorous validation runs less often.

sysd-reliab-211.title: Point-in-time recovery: time travel for data
sysd-reliab-211.text: Point-in-time recovery restores each affected artifact to its own unique point in time, possibly for millions of users across days, weeks or months. Google calls it time-travel. A solution that offers it across ACID and BASE datastores, while meeting strict uptime, latency, scale, velocity and cost goals, is a chimera today. Building it yourself costs velocity. Many projects compromise with a tiered backup strategy, such as days of costly local snapshots plus full and incremental copies every two days. Gradual losses may take days to notice, so recovery needs snapshots from further back. Merging restored data with the current state significantly complicates the restore.

sysd-reliab-225.title: Least-loaded round robin: send work where requests are fewest
sysd-reliab-225.text: In least-loaded round robin, each client tracks its active requests to every backend in its subset and round robins among the backends with the fewest. Loaded tasks tend to be slower, so the policy moves load away from them. An unhealthy task may fast-fail with 100% errors and attract traffic because it looks lightly loaded; counting recent errors as active requests fixes this. The active-request count is also a poor proxy for capability, since a backend twice as fast may look equally loaded. Each client sees only its own requests, and in practice large services see the most loaded backend using twice the CPU of the least loaded.

sysd-reliab-226.title: Weighted round robin: backends report how they are doing
sysd-reliab-226.text: What if backends told clients how busy they are? In weighted round robin, they do. Each client keeps a capability score per backend and distributes requests round robin in proportion to those scores. Backends include their observed queries per second, errors per second and utilization in each response, health-check replies included. Clients adjust the scores from each backend's successful requests and utilization cost, with a penalty for failures. In practice it worked very well, drastically narrowing the spread between the most and least loaded tasks after clients switched from least-loaded round robin. The difficulty is that clients decide in real time with only partial or stale backend state.
